analogy.p: Imagine you have exactly one coin of each of these values: 1p, 2p, 4p, 8p, 16p, 32p, 64p and 128p. Any amount from 0p up to 255p can be paid exactly by choosing which coins to use, and each coin is either in your pile (1) or not (0). The binary number is just a record of which coins you used. Converting denary to binary is working out which coins to pick (always starting with the biggest one that fits), and binary to denary is adding up the coins in your pile. The analogy breaks down because with real money you could use several coins of the same value, but in binary each place value can be used only once (0 or 1).
analogy.t: Coins that can only be used once

bullets: **Denary** (decimal) is **base 10**: it uses the digits 0 to 9 and each place is worth 10 times the place to its right.
**Binary** is **base 2**: it uses only 0 and 1 and each place is worth 2 times the place to its right.
You must be able to convert **binary to denary** and **denary to binary** for numbers up to 8 bits (0 to 255).
Conversions are worth marks in short questions (often 1 to 2 marks each) and are also used inside longer questions on hexadecimal, shifts and image/sound file sizes.
Showing **working** is wise: a correct method with an arithmetic slip can still earn a mark.
The topic has no tricks, only accuracy, so practise until it is automatic.
core.h: What you need to know and why binary matters
core.p: OCR J277 (section 2.6, data representation) expects you to **convert positive whole numbers between binary and denary**, using up to 8 bits (0 to 255). This is a core skill that appears in almost every Paper 2 and is the basis for hexadecimal, binary addition, shifts, text, images and sound. All data in a computer, whether numbers, text, pictures or sound, is stored as **binary**, a number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1. Denary is the ordinary number system that people use. A computer needs binary because its components work with two states, and you need to be able to convert between the two systems accurately.

bullets: Digital circuits use **two states** (on/off, high/low voltage), which are represented as 1 and 0.
Two-state systems are **more reliable** than systems with many voltage levels, because small changes in voltage do not cause a wrong reading.
Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) work on binary values, so processors can do arithmetic and comparisons with them.
Everything is stored as binary: numbers, text characters, images, sound and program instructions.
A **bit** is a single binary digit (0 or 1); it is the smallest unit of data.
Humans prefer denary, so conversion is needed when we enter numbers or read the results; the computer converts internally.
Exam phrase: 'computers use binary because they are made of electronic components (transistors) that have two states, on and off'.
core.p: Computers are built from millions of tiny electronic switches called **transistors** in their processors and memory. A transistor can be either on or off, meaning current is flowing or not. Two states are easy for a circuit to produce and to tell apart, even if there is some electrical noise, so using 1 for 'on' and 0 for 'off' makes the hardware **simple, reliable and cheap**. Storage devices use the same idea: a magnetic region can face one of two ways, a flash memory cell is charged or not, and an optical disc has pits and flat areas. Any piece of data can be represented by a pattern of 1s and 0s.

bullets: Denary 346 means 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 6 units: 300 + 40 + 6.
Binary 1011 means 1 eight + 0 four + 1 two + 1 one: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 in denary.
Binary uses **base 2**, denary **base 10**, and hexadecimal **base 16** (covered in the next spec point).
In any base, the rightmost column is worth 1 (the base to the power 0).
Moving one place left multiplies the column value by the base: by 10 in denary, by 2 in binary.
A binary number needs **more digits** than the same denary number: 255 is three digits in denary but 11111111 (eight digits) in binary.
Always label the base if there could be confusion, for example 1011 (binary) is 11 (denary), not one thousand and eleven.
core.h: Number bases: denary and binary compared
core.p: A **number base** tells you how many different digits are used and how the value of each column grows. In denary, the columns from the right are 1, 10, 100, 1000 and so on (powers of ten). In binary the columns from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and so on (powers of two). Both systems work exactly the same way: the value of a number is the **sum of each digit multiplied by its column value (place value)**. Because binary digits are only 0 or 1, each column is either included (1) or not included (0).

bullets: The place values are: **128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1** (each is double the one on its right).
The leftmost bit is the **most significant bit (MSB)**: it has the biggest value (128 in 8 bits).
The rightmost bit is the **least significant bit (LSB)**: it is worth 1 and decides whether the number is odd or even.
Add up only the columns that contain a 1; ignore the 0 columns.
Learn to write the row of place values quickly at the top of the working space before starting each question.
The doubling pattern also helps you work out other values: 2^8 = 256, 2^9 = 512, 2^10 = 1024.
core.h: Binary place values and the 8-bit table
core.p: For GCSE you work with **8-bit** numbers, so you need to know the eight place values by heart: **128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1**. These are the powers of two from 2^7 down to 2^0. Write them above the binary number to line up the digits. Each 1 means 'add that place value'; each 0 means 'do not add it'. Because there are exactly eight columns, the largest number is when all eight bits are 1.

bullets: 1 bit = a single 0 or 1.
1 nibble = **4 bits** (e.g. 1010).
2 nibbles = 1 byte, so an 8-bit number can be split into two nibbles (0110 1101).
To convert bytes to bits, **multiply by 8**; to convert bits to bytes, **divide by 8**. For example 5 bytes = 40 bits and 64 bits = 8 bytes.
An 8-bit register or character code can hold 256 different values.
Using the right unit matters in exams: do not write 'bytes' when the answer is in bits.
core.p: The size of a binary number is measured in bits. A **bit** is one binary digit. A **nibble** is a group of **4 bits**, and a **byte** is a group of **8 bits**. The byte is the standard unit for storing a single character or one small number, which is why 8-bit conversions are so common in GCSE. A nibble is useful because exactly one nibble can be written as one hexadecimal digit. You should be comfortable saying how many bits are in a given number of bytes and vice versa, because file-size questions use these units.

bullets: 1 bit: 2 values (0 to 1); 2 bits: 4 values (0 to 3); 3 bits: 8 values (0 to 7); 4 bits: 16 values (0 to 15); 8 bits: 256 values (0 to 255).
Number of different values with n bits = **2^n**.
Largest denary value with n bits = **2^n - 1** (all bits set to 1).
Adding one bit **doubles** the number of values, which is why a small increase in bits gives a big increase in range.
The largest 8-bit number is **11111111 = 255**, and the smallest is **00000000 = 0**.
The number 256 cannot be stored in 8 bits; it needs 9 bits (100000000).
GCSE questions on this section use positive whole numbers only (no negative or fractional numbers).
core.h: The range of an n-bit binary number
core.p: With n bits, each bit can be 0 or 1 independently, so there are **2^n different bit patterns**. Because one pattern is used for zero, the largest positive whole number is **2^n - 1**. For 8 bits that is 2^8 - 1 = 256 - 1 = **255**, so an 8-bit unsigned number covers **0 to 255**. Every extra bit **doubles** the number of values you can represent. This idea is used when deciding how many bits are needed for a task, and later for the number of colours in an image (colour depth) and the number of sound levels (bit depth).

bullets: **Step 1:** write the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above the 8 bits.
**Step 2:** write the bits underneath, one per column (add leading zeros if there are fewer than eight).
**Step 3:** for each 1, take the place value; ignore columns with a 0.
**Step 4:** add up the chosen place values to get the denary answer.
Example 11111111: add all place values = **255**.
Check: if the last bit is 1 your answer must be odd; if it is 0 the answer must be even.
core.p: To convert **binary to denary**, write the place values above the digits, find every column that contains a 1, and add those place values. This is the easier direction and is a good way to check an answer that was found by converting the other way. The method is the same for any number of bits, but for 8-bit numbers always write out all eight place values to avoid slipping a column. If the binary number has fewer than 8 digits, add leading zeros so the units column lines up under the 1.

bullets: **Step 1:** write the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 across the page.
**Step 2:** start with 128. If the number is **greater than or equal to** the place value, write 1 and subtract; otherwise write 0.
**Step 3:** carry the remainder to the next place value and repeat until you reach 1.
**Step 4:** the row of 1s and 0s is the answer; the remainder at the end must be 0.
Example, 200: 128 fits (rem 72); 64 fits (rem 8); 32 no; 16 no; 8 fits (rem 0); 4, 2, 1 no. Answer **11001000**.
Example, 156: 128 fits (rem 28); 64 no; 32 no; 16 fits (rem 12); 8 fits (rem 4); 4 fits (rem 0); 2 no; 1 no. Answer **10011100**.
Check by converting back: 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 156.
Common slip: forgetting to write a 0 for a place value that does not fit, which shifts all the later digits.
core.h: Converting denary to binary: the subtraction (place value) method
core.p: The most popular method for 8-bit numbers is to work through the place values from the **largest to the smallest**. At each place ask: 'does this place value fit into the number I have left?' If yes, write 1 and subtract it; if no, write 0 and move on. When the remainder reaches 0, any remaining columns are 0. This method keeps the bits in the right order automatically because you write them left to right.

bullets: **Step 1:** divide the denary number by 2 and write down the quotient (whole number) and the remainder (0 or 1).
**Step 2:** divide the quotient by 2 again and note the remainder; repeat until the quotient is 0.
**Step 3:** read the remainders **from bottom to top**; that is the binary number.
**Step 4:** if the answer must be 8 bits, add leading zeros on the left.
Common slip: reading the remainders from the top down, which gives the number backwards.
core.h: Converting denary to binary: the repeated division method
core.p: A second method is to **divide the number by 2 repeatedly** and record the remainder each time. You keep dividing the whole-number result by 2 until you reach 0. The remainders are the bits of the binary number, but they are produced from the **least significant bit first**, so you read them **from the bottom up**. This method works for any size of number and some students find it quicker. It is acceptable in an exam; the mark scheme gives the answer, not the method, unless the question asks to show working.

bullets: Check 1: **convert back** to denary and see if you get the starting number.
Check 2: **odd/even**: an odd denary number must end in 1 in binary and an even number in 0.
Check 3: **size**: if the number is 128 or more, the leftmost bit must be 1; if it is less than 128 it must be 0.
Check 4: the binary number must have exactly 8 digits when asked for an 8-bit answer.
Shortcut: for numbers close to 255, take the complement: 255 - 5 = 250, so 250 is 11111111 with the bits for 5 (101) flipped, giving 11111010.
Do not rush: an arithmetic error in subtraction is the most common reason for losing marks.
core.h: Choosing a method and checking your answer
core.p: Both methods give the same answer, so use whichever you are more accurate with. Many top-scoring students use the subtraction method for 8-bit numbers and the division method as a check. **Always check** your answer by converting back to denary, which takes only a few seconds and catches most slips. Another quick check is whether the number is odd or even, which is shown by the last bit.

bullets: Leading zeros **do not change the value** but are needed when an exact number of bits is requested.
Write binary digits clearly; confusing a 0 with a 6 or a 1 with a 7 loses marks.
If asked to 'convert 13 to an 8-bit binary number' the answer is **00001101**.
Grouping in 4s (nibbles) makes long numbers easier to check.
If a question gives you a binary number with fewer than 8 digits, add leading zeros in the working to line up the place values.
Do not add trailing zeros (on the right): that **would** change the value (it doubles it for each extra zero).
Include units or the base when needed, such as 'the denary equivalent is 13'.
core.h: Leading zeros and presentation of answers
core.p: Leading zeros (zeros on the left) do not change the value of a binary number: 00001101 and 1101 both equal 13. However, if a question asks for an **8-bit** binary number you must write all eight digits, including the leading zeros, otherwise the mark may be lost. Keep the digits evenly spaced and in clear groups so they are easy to read. Some students group them in nibbles (0000 1101), which is acceptable and often clearer.

bullets: Largest number in 6 bits = 2^6 - 1 = 64 - 1 = **63**.
To store 100: 6 bits hold up to 63, 7 bits hold up to 127, so **7 bits** are needed.
To store 300: 8 bits only reach 255, so **9 bits** are needed (up to 511).
Number of values in 5 bits = 2^5 = **32** (0 to 31).
A question may ask how many different values a certain number of bits can represent: use **2^n**.
Remember 'values' counts zero; 'largest number' is one less.
core.h: How many bits are needed? Working backwards
core.p: Questions sometimes ask for the **smallest number of bits** needed to store a given denary value, or for the largest number that can be stored in a given number of bits. To find the number of bits for a value, find the smallest power of two that is greater than the value (so that 2^n - 1 is at least the value). For example 100 is bigger than 63 (6 bits) but not bigger than 127 (7 bits), so 7 bits are needed. These ideas lead directly to the later topics of colour depth, bit depth and the number of characters in a character set.

bullets: **Hexadecimal (2.6):** each hex digit = one 4-bit nibble; learn binary 0000 to 1111 as 0 to 15.
**Binary addition (2.6):** columns use the same place values, carrying when 1 + 1 = 10 in binary.
**Binary shifts (2.6):** a left shift by one place multiplies by 2; a right shift divides by 2 (ignoring the remainder).
**ASCII and Unicode (2.6):** each character is stored as a binary code, 7 or 8 bits in ASCII.
**Images (2.6):** the colour depth is the number of bits per pixel, which sets the number of colours as 2^n.
**Sound (2.6):** the bit depth is the number of bits for each sample.
**Paper 1 (CPU and memory):** instructions and addresses are all binary numbers; memory addresses use binary values too.
**Networks:** an IPv4 address contains four numbers from 0 to 255, each an 8-bit binary value (a byte).
core.p: Binary and denary conversion is the foundation for many other parts of the specification. Hexadecimal is a shorthand for binary: each hex digit stands for a nibble, so converting between binary and hex relies on being fluent with 4-bit numbers. Binary addition uses the same place values, and binary shifts multiply or divide by powers of two. Image and sound data are stored as binary numbers, and file-size calculations use the number of bits. Other areas, such as ASCII and Unicode, use binary codes to represent characters.

exam: 'Convert the binary number 10110101 to denary' is usually 1 to 2 marks: write the place values above the bits and show the addition for method marks. The answer is 181.
'Convert the denary number to 8-bit binary' is typically 1 to 2 marks: give all 8 digits; a correct method with a slip can still earn one mark.
Always write the place values 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above your working; it takes seconds and prevents column errors.
Check by converting back; if it does not match the original number, find the error before moving on.
A 'State why computers use binary' question earns the mark for 'transistors / electronic switches have two states, on and off' (1 mark), plus a link to 1 and 0.
For 'what is the largest number that can be stored in n bits', use 2^n - 1 and show the calculation.
Bits/bytes questions: show the multiplication or division by 8 and give the unit.
If a table of values is given, check whether the question wants binary to denary or the other way round before starting.
Questions on hexadecimal and shifts often start with a binary conversion, so accurate conversion gains marks in later parts too.
Practise until a conversion takes under a minute; speed gives time for harder 6-mark questions.
Write digits clearly and keep a consistent size so the examiner can read them.

mistakes.r: The place values double each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.
Add leading zeros so the answer has exactly 8 digits (e.g. 00001101).
mistakes.w: Writing a binary answer with fewer than 8 digits when 8 bits are asked for.

mistakes.r: Read the remainders from the bottom to the top (last remainder first).
mistakes.w: Reading the remainders from top to bottom in the division method.

mistakes.r: The largest is 2^8 - 1 = 255; 256 is the number of different values (0 to 255).
Write a 0 for every place value that does not fit so all eight columns are filled.
mistakes.w: Skipping a place value that does not fit and not writing a 0.

mistakes.r: Only add the place values that have a 1 under them.
mistakes.w: Adding all the place values, not just those with a 1.

mistakes.r: Computers use binary because transistors have two states, on and off.
mistakes.w: Saying computers use binary because it is faster or easier for people.

mistakes.r: A bit is one binary digit, a nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits.
mistakes.w: Mixing up bits and bytes (e.g. 'a byte is 4 bits').

mistakes.r: Add zeros on the left; zeros on the right change the value.
mistakes.w: Adding zeros on the right to make 8 digits.

summary: You must convert positive whole numbers between binary and denary (up to 8 bits, 0 to 255) and know why computers use binary. This is the foundation of hexadecimal, binary addition, shifts, text, images and sound, so accuracy here earns marks across Paper 2.

terms.d: The base 10 number system using the digits 0 to 9; the number system humans normally use.
The base 2 number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1.
A single binary digit, either 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data.
The value of a digit's column in a number; in binary the columns are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.
The number of different digits used in a number system, which is also the multiplier between neighbouring columns.
The leftmost bit of a binary number, which has the greatest place value.
The rightmost bit of a binary number, which has the lowest place value (1).
A zero placed at the left of a binary number which does not change its value.
A tiny electronic switch in a processor that is either on or off, representing 1 or 0.
The amount left over after a division; in the division method the remainders form the binary digits.
A binary number with 8 digits that can represent the denary values 0 to 255.
A number found by multiplying 2 by itself a number of times (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...).
A number with no sign; only zero and positive whole numbers.

worked.ans: (a) 63 [1 mark]. (b) 7 bits [2 marks: 1 for showing 6 bits is not enough or 127, 1 for the answer].
worked.q: (a) State the largest denary number that can be stored in 6 bits. (b) What is the smallest number of bits needed to store the number 100? [3]
steps: (a) With 6 bits there are 2^6 = 64 patterns, so the values are 0 to 63. Largest = 2^6 - 1 = 63.
(b) 6 bits can only reach 63, which is less than 100.
7 bits reach 2^7 - 1 = 127, which is at least 100.
So 7 bits are needed. Check: 100 = 1100100 in binary, which has 7 digits (64 + 32 + 4 = 100).
